subject: Canada's retail gain was mostly the price of gas
bodyMarkdown:
If you read only the headline, Canadians went shopping in September. Look at what they actually carried home and the picture flips, which is worth your time because the Bank of Canada sets rates again in 18 days.

## What Friday's numbers said

Statistics Canada reported on Friday that retail sales rose 0.8 per cent in September to $75.3 billion. Almost all of it came from one line. Sales at gasoline stations and fuel vendors jumped 6.9 per cent. In volume terms, meaning after price changes are stripped out, sales rose 0.1 per cent. **Core retail sales**, which leave out gas stations, fuel vendors and car dealers, also rose 0.1 per cent. General merchandise retailers gained 1.5 per cent, food and beverage retailers fell 0.4 per cent, and e-commerce slipped 0.2 per cent to $5.7 billion, or 7.5 per cent of all retail trade. Sales rose in nine provinces. So September was a price story wearing a demand costume. Reuters reported on Friday that the agency's **advance estimate**, an early reading built from partial survey responses, points to sales falling 1.5 per cent in October, the biggest monthly drop since February 2025.

## Why the Bank raised rates anyway

Here is the part that confuses people I talk to. Spending is flat, and the Bank of Canada still took its policy rate to 2.50 per cent from 2.25 per cent on October 28, the first increase since July 2023. The reason is fuel. Statistics Canada reported on Monday that inflation held at 3.1 per cent in October, under the 3.2 per cent economists in a Reuters poll expected, with gasoline up 30.9 per cent from a year earlier and energy overall up 21.8 per cent. The Bank's published summary of Governing Council deliberations says it moved to cut the risk that persistently high energy prices spread into other prices. Core measures are calmer: CPI-median at 2.0 per cent, CPI-trim at 1.8. Governing Council said it might need to go further and would decide one meeting at a time. Prime at the big banks went to about 4.70 per cent, the number sitting on your variable mortgage.

## What I think happens on December 9

A hold. CBC reported on Monday that CIBC economist Andrew Grantham read the inflation numbers as fitting his call for no move next month, and Friday's retail report gives the Bank more cover to wait, not less. My own read is that the Bank hiked into an energy shock it does not control, and now it has to hope the shock fades before the consumer does. Pump prices already fell 2.5 per cent during October and kept falling in November, so the arithmetic that pushed headline inflation to 3.1 per cent starts running in reverse early next year. TD Economics still expects one more quarter-point hike in the first quarter of 2027, taking the rate to 2.75 per cent. I would not count on that if the October retail drop survives revision.

## The takeaway

Governor Tiff Macklem speaks Tuesday in Toronto to the Economic Club of Canada, and that press conference is the last real signal before December 9, so listen for whether he treats the fuel spike as a one-off or as something leaking into other prices. He announced on November 16 that he will not seek a second term when his ends on June 2, 2027, which means this winter's calls are the ones he will be remembered for. If you carry a variable mortgage or a line of credit, budget off prime near 4.70 per cent and assume it stays there well into next year instead of falling. And when the October retail number lands for real, skip the headline and go straight to the volumes line.
